catalog_quote: ACCENT. La langue banda est chantée, c'est-à-dire, que chaque syllabe a sa tonalité propre, et est prononcée sur un ton plus élevé ou plus bas que la voisine. On distingue trois tons principaux : le ton haut, dans nó, dí, ká, tout, le ton moyen, dans enji, ils, le ton bas, dans mbwạngạ, palabre. Nous ne noterons ici la tonalité des éléments du langage que dans la mesure où la fonction du mot dans la phrase la fait varier : Le substantif verbal, joint au verbe, fait élever la tonalité de la voyelle de celui-ci : tee fú'fu, il est beau, en face de tee fu wa, id.; lobạn gé'gere, le pagne est grand, en face de lobạn gere wa. En dehors de l'accent de hauteur, il existe en banda un accent d'intensité qui affecte certaines syllabes des mots, en sorte que les syllabes non accentuées s'abrègent et ont une tendance à disparaître : Bĕleda, tronc d'arbre, bleda; temŏ, marque du futur, tem; marœ̆, f…

new_statements.translation: ACCENT. The Banda language is sung, that is, each syllable has its own tonality and is pronounced on a higher or lower tone than its neighbour. Three main tones are distinguished: the high tone, in nó, dí, ká 'all'; the mid tone, in enji 'they'; the low tone, in mbwạnga 'palaver'. [...] Apart from the pitch accent, there exists in Banda an intensity accent which affects certain syllables of words, so that the unaccented syllables shorten and tend to disappear: Bèleda 'tree trunk', bleda; temö, future marker, tem; marœ 'to do', mar.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the two page images myself: and (Google Books H1cOAAAAYAAJ, 'Digitalisiert von Google' footer; running heads 'PHONÉTIQUE 23' / '24 ESSAI DE GRAMMAIRE BANDA'; title page PP7 = 'Travaux et Mémoires de l'Institut d'Ethnologie XIII, R. P. Charles Tisserant, Essai sur la grammaire Banda, Paris, Institut d'Ethnologie, 1930'). The quoted passage is there verbatim: p. 23 heading 'ACCENT.' then 'La langue banda est chantée, c'est-à-dire, que chaque syllabe a sa tonalité propre, et est prononcée sur un ton plus élevé ou plus bas que la voisine. On distingue trois tons principaux : le ton haut, dans nó, dí, ká, tout, le ton moyen, dans enji, ils, le ton bas, dans mbwạnga, palabre.' -- the reade…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Banda is a three-level register tone language (every syllable carries a high, mid or low tone). In addition Tisserant posits an intensity accent ('accent d'intensité') on certain syllables of the word; he gives no rule for its position, only its effect: unaccented syllables shorten and tend to drop (initial pretonic vowel in Bèleda > bleda; final vowel in temö > tem, marœ > mar).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for the intensity accent; tone (not stress) is the primary contrast and is said to vary with the word's function in the sentence (p. 23).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('certaines syllabes des mots'), citation forms; the intensity accent is described only through reduction/elision of unaccented syllables, no position rule. The same pages note that in speech and drum language words run together in phrase groups ('groupes de mots accouplés'), and that loanwords 'reçoivent leurs accents tout comme les mots banda authentiques' (p. 24).
new_statements.identity_note: Tisserant 1930 is a multidialectal 'Banda' grammar. His base 'dialecte banda' (pp. 3-4) is the principal group (Linda, Banda-Banda, Togbo, Moruba, Ngao, Wada.. = today lind1250, togb1241 etc.); Langwasi (lang1318), Dakpwa (= West Central Banda west2458/bbp, with Gbaga-Nord and Gbi, p. 5) and Vora are treated as distinct 'dialectes' that get separate remarks (pp. 21-22, 40). The ACCENT statement (pp. 23-24) is made for 'la langue banda' as a whole, not for Dakpwa specifically. Glottolog 5.3 attaches the work to togb1241, lang1318 and west2458 (Hammarström's note: 'mainly Banda-Togbo.. but a lot of Langwasi and Dakpwa'). Sister-language data for comparison: Cotel 1907 (Togbo, togb1241) p. XI 'accent le plus souvent sur l'avant-dernière syllabe' + three tones; Sampson 1985 (Tangbago, band1345) and Althabégoïty 2024 (Ngbugu) tone only, no stress. PHOIBLE GM 1308 and Wikipedia's bbp phonology are actually Sampson's Tangbago data.

new_statements.quote: 2a. There appear to be three main tone levels in these languages—High, Mid, and Low. [...] 2b. Stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length. In MAYOGO there is a tendency towards vowel length on the penultimate syllable. In NGBAKA, GBAYA, and BANDA, on the other hand, there is a tendency towards extra shortness here. Compare Eboué's BANDA spellings yavro (dog), yabru (goat), akblo (child) with Hackett's TOGBO renderings yavor6 [scanned; = yavoro], aboro, agbolo.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Tisserant statement (tone language, three tones, plus an intensity accent under which unaccented syllables shorten): it adds that the shortening targets the penultimate syllable in Banda. Says nothing about placement and never names the West Central (Dakpa) dialects; 'BANDA' here is Eboué's Oubangui-Chari material and Hackett's Togbo.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi languages: three level tones (High, Mid, Low); stress is mentioned only as a cause of vowel-quality and vowel-length changes, and in Banda the penultimate syllable tends to be extra short (Eboué's yavro/yabru/akblo vs Togbo yavoro/aboro/agbolo). No rule for where word stress falls is given.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the archive.org copy is controlled lending (/pdf not reachable by automated download, search-inside 403), so only full-text-search highlight windows were read; 'Dakpa', 'Dakpwa', 'Gbaga', 'Langwasi', 'Vidiri', 'Wojo' return 0 hits in the scanned index, and 'BANDA stress' as a phrase returns 0 hits, so this p. 86 sentence is the only stress remark touching Banda that the index exposes.
new_statements.identity_note: Neither opened work describes West Central Banda (Dakpa) specifically. Tisserant 1930 states the ACCENT passage for 'la langue banda' as a whole, i.e. his principal dialect group (Linda, Banda-Banda, Togbo, Moruba, Ngao, Wada, pp. 3-5), while Dakpwa/Gbaga-Nord/Gbi (= bbp) are a separate 'dialecte dakpwa' with their own remarks (pp. 21-22, 29-40); Glottolog attaches the grammar to togb1241, lang1318 and west2458. Tucker & Bryan 1966 speak at the level of the Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi group, with 'BANDA' = Eboué's spellings and 'TOGBO' = Hackett's material; 'Dakpa', 'Dakpwa', 'Gbaga', 'Langwasi', 'Vidiri', 'Wojo' return no hits in the book's scanned index.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the source of the existing statement; the quote is the same passage, verified on the page images and extended to the end of the intensity-accent sentence on p. 24. Identity caveat: Tisserant's 'la langue banda' is his principal dialect (Linda, Banda-Banda, Togbo, Ngao, Wada.., pp. 3-5); Dakpwa, Gbaga and Gbi are listed as a separate 'dialecte dakpwa' (p. 4 'DIALECTE DAKPWA', remarks pp. 21-22), and the ACCENT statement is not marked as Dakpwa-specific.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Banda is a three-tone language (high, mid, low); in addition there is a stress (intensity) accent on certain syllables, and the unstressed syllables shorten and can drop (Bèleda > bleda, temö > tem, marœ > mar). No position for the stress is stated; the examples show the retained syllable being the first (Bè-, te-, ma-) but Tisserant gives no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: none; whole-book a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned: 'accent' occurs only on pp. 23-24 (the other hits are 'accentua' p. 9 = migration and 'peu accentuées' p. 20 = vowel quality), so this is the book's only word-accent statement.
